findings.source_passage: On the last afternoon before he went abroad, he sat with Daisy in his arms for a long, silent time.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning "On the last afternoon before he went abroad" (mid-chapter)
findings.why_it_matters: This hushed, lyrical memory is the only sustained scene of quiet intimacy between Gatsby and Daisy; cutting it removes a key emotional counter-weight to the later disillusion.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full paragraph, keeping the fire-lit stillness, Daisy’s flushed cheeks, and the tactile gestures (brushed lips, finger-tips) in Fitzgerald’s cadence.

findings.source_passage: Her porch was bright with the bought luxury of star-shine; the wicker of the settee squeaked fashionably as she turned toward him and he kissed her curious and lovely mouth.
findings.source_locator: after "When they met again, two days later"
findings.why_it_matters: The prosodic flourish "bought luxury of star-shine" and the sensual detail of the squeaking wicker are quintessential Fitzgerald; their removal flattens Nick’s narrative music and Gatsby’s recollection.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-insert the sentence verbatim (or at most with minimal trimming) to preserve the distinctive imagery and rhythm.

findings.source_passage: He felt their presence all about the house, pervading the air with the shades and echoes of still vibrant emotions.
findings.source_locator: end of the long Daisy-house description (early Louisville section)
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence clinches the class/sex aura surrounding Daisy by literalising past lovers as ‘shades and echoes’; losing it weakens the social-spectral motif scholars note.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the line to complete the atmospheric build-up of the Daisy-house passage.

summary: Three voice-laden, interpretively important sentences are missing; restore them to avoid flattening Gatsby’s Louisville back-story.
